The Wisconsin State Law Library puts it plainly, saying there is no agreed-upon age when a child can stay home safely, and most places leave the call to parents. So the decision rests on three separate things: what your local law permits, how your child behaves when small problems come up, and what you're actually asking of them. Twenty minutes at 4pm is a different ask than a whole evening. Age gives you a starting point and nothing more. Print out the following image a few times, fill it out the first few times your kids are home alone so they've got everything they need written down: What age can a child stay home alone according to child health guidance Child health organizations tend to land on 11 or 12 for a short stretch alone during the day. Where your state, county, or country names an age in statute, that number governs, whatever any organization advises. And no single age can answer the follow-up questions, which are the ones that matter more: how long, what time of day, whether a younger sibling is in the house, and who your child reaches if the power cuts out. So when you ask what age can my child stay home alone, hold the 11-to-12 range as a rough floor for a first short trial rather than a green light. A handful do, with Illinois setting the highest threshold in the country at 14 and others sitting anywhere from six upward.
